lessons.title: Generating Unique Symbols with Symbol()
lessons.description: Symbols are unique, immutable primitive values — perfect for hidden object keys and metadata.

sections.heading: What is a Symbol?
paragraphs: A Symbol is a unique, immutable primitive value. Every Symbol() call creates a new, distinct value — even with the same description. They're primarily used as object property keys.
list: Symbol("description") — creates a symbol with a helpful label
Two symbols with the same description are still different

codeExamples.heading: Creating and using symbols
explanation: Every Symbol() call creates a truly unique value.
Symbols as object keys are hidden from normal iteration (for...in, Object.keys).
You must store the symbol reference to access symbol-keyed properties.
This creates truly private properties without #private syntax.

practice.task: Create two symbols with the same description and verify they're different. Then use one as an object key and access its value.
hints: Create: let a = Symbol("test"); let b = Symbol("test").

keyTakeaways: Every Symbol() call creates a unique value — even with the same description.
Symbols as object keys are hidden from normal enumeration.
You must store the symbol reference to access its properties.
Symbols are useful for metadata, hidden properties and protocol methods.
lessons.challenge: Use symbols to add hidden metadata to objects that can't be accidentally overwritten or accessed by external code.

lessons.title: Global Symbol Registry: Symbol.for() & Symbol.keyFor()
lessons.description: Create shared symbols across different parts of your application using the global registry.

sections.heading: The global symbol registry
paragraphs: Sometimes you need the same symbol in different files or modules. Symbol.for() creates or retrieves symbols from a global registry.
list: Symbol.for("key") — creates or returns a shared symbol
Symbol.keyFor(symbol) — returns the registry key for a symbol
Same key always returns the same symbol

codeExamples.heading: Global symbol registry
explanation: Symbol.for() looks up the global registry — same key returns the same symbol.
This lets different modules share symbols for cross-module communication.
Symbol.keyFor() returns the registry key, useful for debugging.
Regular Symbol() doesn't use the registry — only Symbol.for() does.

practice.task: Create a shared symbol using Symbol.for() in two different script sections. Verify they're the same symbol and can be used to share data.

keyTakeaways: Symbol.for() creates or retrieves symbols from a global registry.
Same key always returns the same symbol — enables cross-module sharing.
Symbol.keyFor() returns the registry key for a given symbol.
Use global symbols when different parts of your app need to share a symbol.
lessons.challenge: Build a plugin system where plugins register themselves using a shared Symbol.for() key.

lessons.title: Customizing Engine Hooks via Well-Known Symbols (Symbol.iterator)
lessons.description: Well-known Symbols let you customize how JavaScript engines interact with your objects.

sections.heading: Well-known Symbols
paragraphs: JavaScript has built-in Symbol constants that control engine behavior. Implementing them on your objects hooks into language features like iteration, string conversion and matching.
list: Symbol.iterator — makes an object iterable with for...of

codeExamples.heading: Custom iteration with Symbol.iterator
explanation: Implementing Symbol.iterator makes your object work with for...of.
The iterator must return an object with a next() method.
next() returns { value, done } — done is true when iteration is complete.
This also enables spread operator and destructuring.

practice.task: Create a Fibonacci class that implements Symbol.iterator to yield the first N Fibonacci numbers when used with for...of.
hints: Track the current and next Fibonacci numbers.
Return { value, done: false } for each number.

keyTakeaways: Well-known Symbols hook into JavaScript engine behavior.
Symbol.iterator makes objects work with for...of, spread and destructuring.
The iterator protocol requires a next() method returning { value, done }.
These hooks let you make custom objects behave like built-in types.
lessons.challenge: Create a Range class that supports for...of, spread, destructuring and .map() by implementing Symbol.iterator.
